source.title: Predicting Multi-View Rashomon Representation: Can We Learn Where Models Disagree?
source.authors: Ming-Yue Ma; Zong-Bo Han; Chang-Qing Zhang; Guang-Yu Wang

record.tranche_reason: The study measures sample-level cross-model neighborhood agreement with a different similarity method and examines how it varies across inputs and distribution shifts; it does not test convergence as a function of model scale or capability.
record.gate_note: The reported Pearson correlations measure how well a predictor estimates measured neighborhood agreement; they are not themselves measurements of convergence strength. The study also explicitly reports input-dependent agreement and increasing neighborhood divergence under more severe Gaussian corruption. Results of cited work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study measures sample-level cross-model k-NN overlap (cosine, k=50) among frozen vision encoders. It reports that agreement varies across inputs and that neighborhoods diverge under heavier Gaussian noise. This bears weakly on the input/OOD part of V6. Most results (r1–r33) measure how well a predictor estimates agreement, not how strong convergence is.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that inter-model representational disagreement is structured, input-dependent, and partly encoded in single representations, so it can be predicted efficiently and tracks downstream risk. They note the mapping becomes unreliable under severe corruption.
record.recipe_differences: Uses sample-level cosine nearest-neighbor overlap and predicts that score from one model's representation; it does not reproduce a scale sweep or the original studies' convergence measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Prediction correlation varies across external datasets and corruption severity, and across comparison-model compositions and anchor choices. Predictor architecture also affects prediction accuracy. The principal agreement measurement fixes cosine similarity and k=50.

fits_no_version.finding: A lightweight predictor using one model's representation estimates cross-model neighborhood agreement (Pearson r about 0.70–0.77 in-distribution, 0.39–0.73 under shift, 0.578 leave-anchor-out).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sample-level cross-model representational agreement is partly encoded in, and predictable from, a single model's representation.

record.problems: The main agreement measure uses one similarity metric (cosine) and one neighborhood size (k=50), so metric and neighborhood-size sensitivity are not assessed. Several results concern prediction accuracy rather than agreement magnitude. The text gives no uncertainty estimates for the reported table correlations.
record.rows_left_out: Predictor-architecture comparison results in Table 5, computational costs in Table 6, downstream-risk correlations in Table 7, and reference-set-size results in Figure 6 were omitted because they concern predictor design, efficiency, downstream association, or data requirements rather than cross-model convergence itself. Figure 7's downstream probe-accuracy breakdown was also omitted.

untested.parts: No scale or capability sweep; all models are base-size.
Only image encoders; no image–caption pairing.
No seed replicates of one architecture.
No mapping, stitching or relative-representation test.
Similarity metric (cosine) and neighborhood size (k=50) are fixed; metric and k dependence are not tested. Aggregate agreement magnitudes per dataset or shift are not reported.
No plateau analysis or attribution to shared data or objectives.

record.verdict_notes: The study's framing (substantial disagreement among foundation models) runs against strong convergence, but it never quantifies overall agreement levels, so no V1/V7 verdict is possible. Its V6 evidence concerns per-sample variation and qualitative OOD divergence, a weak and indirect test.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size or capability sweep, and no test of whether cross-model alignment rises with scale or performance.
No paired image-caption representation comparison or test of alignment as vision and language models improve.
No comparison of independently trained seeds of the same architecture or analysis of shared features or subspaces.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired interchangeability test.
No test for recurring interpretable features, neurons, or circuits.

Tests input and distribution dependence of neighborhood agreement, including Gaussian corruption. It fixes cosine similarity and k=50 in the main experiments and does not compare alternative similarity metrics or neighborhood sizes.
Does not quantify whether alignment plateaus or attribute alignment to shared data or objectives rather than a common model of reality.

rows.subject: CLIP, DINOv2, and ViT-21K
rows.size_stated: CLIP ViT-B/32, DINOv2 ViT-B/14, ViT-B/16; parameter counts not stated
rows.operation_detail: Compare the models' neighborhoods for individual inputs and report input-dependent agreement
rows.measure: Cross-model neighborhood agreement varies across samples; the text describes substantial input-to-input variation
rows.value: The authors state that agreement varies substantially across inputs; no aggregate values stated
rows.note: Directly supports input dependence under the study's neighborhood-overlap measure.
rows.check: Shows per-sample variation in agreement, not that an aggregate convergence score shifts with the input set. No summary numbers for agreement magnitude are given; the evidence is qualitative (Fig. 7) plus text.

rows.subject: CLIP, DINOv2, and ViT-21K
rows.size_stated: CLIP ViT-B/32, DINOv2 ViT-B/14, ViT-B/16; parameter counts not stated
rows.operation_detail: Examine neighborhood divergence and prediction error as Gaussian corruption severity increases
rows.measure: Qualitative neighborhood divergence and absolute prediction error for three examples
rows.value: Neighborhoods are described as increasingly divergent; example absolute errors increase from 0.013 to 0.031 and 0.037
rows.note: The text explicitly describes greater neighborhood divergence at stronger corruption; the example errors are prediction errors, not direct agreement values.
rows.check: Divergence is described qualitatively for three examples only. The quoted numbers (0.013→0.037) are predictor absolute errors, not agreement values. No mean measured NA50 per severity is reported.

relationships.condition: ImageNet-1K inputs; CLIP/DINOv2/ViT-21K; cosine k=50 neighborhood overlap
relationships.reason: Authors report agreement varies substantially across inputs, with high- and low-agreement examples (r34). This is sample-level evidence, not an aggregate shift.
relationships.display_finding: Neighbourhood agreement varied substantially across individual inputs, with both high-agreement and low-agreement examples.

relationships.condition: ImageNet-C Gaussian noise, increasing severity (three qualitative examples)
relationships.reason: Authors state neighborhoods become increasingly divergent as corruption rises (r35). The evidence is qualitative only.
relationships.display_finding: Neighbourhoods became increasingly divergent as Gaussian-noise severity increased in the illustrated examples.
